item.subject: Mathematics
item.stem:
Sam said that 1/3 of a pie is less than 1/4 of the same pie.

Is Sam correct? ____

Use the circles below to show why this is so.

[Image: Two circles]

Shade in 1/3 of this circle

Shade in 1/4 of this circle

descriptors: NO. Both circles are correctly partitioned.
NO. No partitioning is shown.
NO. Only one of the circles correctly partitioned.
NO. Other incorrect ways of partitioning.
YES, or there is no conclusion stated. Both circles are correctly partitioned.
Other partial.
YES. No partitioning is shown.
YES. The part representing 1/3 is made consistently smaller than the part representing 1/4.
YES. Other responses where one or both of the circles partitioned into 3 and/or 4 parts.
Other incorrect.

item.scoring_notes: Note: The partition of circles has priority over shading. This is reflected in the scoring guide below.

reference_items.figure_description:
Five identical squares, labeled A through E, each partitioned and shaded differently:
- Option A: The square is divided horizontally into 5 equal strips. The top 2 strips are shaded grey and the bottom 3 strips are unshaded (white).
- Option B: The square is divided by a diagonal from the bottom-left corner to the top-right corner, and a line segment from the center to the bottom-right corner. The entire upper-left triangular half is shaded grey, the right triangular section is shaded grey, and the bottom triangular section is unshaded.
- Option C: The square is divided by two vertical lines into three strips: a narrow shaded strip on the left, a wide unshaded strip in the middle, and a narrow shaded strip on the right.
- Option D: An unshaded triangle has its base along the entire bottom edge of the square and its apex at the midpoint of the top edge. The two right triangles flanking it on the left and right are shaded grey.
- Option E: The square is divided by two vertical lines into 3 equal-width vertical strips. The left strip and the right strip are shaded grey, and the middle strip is unshaded.

reference_items.subject: Mathematics
reference_items.stem:
Get to 20 Number Game

Two children, Joan and Herbert, are learning to play a game “Get to 20.” Here are the rules for the game.

GET TO 20
RULES

Pick Tiles: Each player draws three number tiles.

Add Tiles: Each player places the three tiles to make an addition problem with the sum total closest to 20.

For example, here are four ways a player who draws [1] , [4] , and [5] could place the tiles:

  [5] [1]          [4] [5]          [1] [5]             [1]
+     [4]    or  +     [1]    or  +     [4]    or     + [5]
---------        ---------        ---------         + [4]
       55               46               19         -----
                                                       10

This player should choose to show the addition problem
  15
+  4
----
  19
because 19 is the total closest to 20.

Joan and Herbert played the game “Get to 20.”

Joan picked [2] , [7] , and [9] . Herbert picked [1] , [3] , and [6] .

C. Herbert said, “If I pick [1] , [4] , and [6] , I can make 20 two different ways.”

Show two ways Herbert could make 20 with [1] , [4] , and [6] .

First way:

Second way:

Only one way correct 16 + 4 OR 14 + 6

At the top is an equilateral triangle with dots at each of its three vertices, labeled "tile" to the right of its right edge.

Below is an irregular polygon drawn on an isometric (triangular) dot grid, with dots marking vertices along its boundary and in its interior:
- Top edge: a horizontal segment 3 units long, with 4 dots evenly spaced (including endpoints).
- Left boundary: from the top-left dot, a line goes down and right by 1 unit to an indented vertex dot; from there, a line goes down and left by 1 unit to the bottom-left corner dot.
- Bottom edge: a horizontal segment 4 units long, with 5 dots evenly spaced (including endpoints).
- Right boundary: from the top-right dot, a line goes down and right by 1 unit to a vertex dot at the middle horizontal level; from that dot, a horizontal line extends right by 1 unit to another vertex dot; from that dot, a line goes down and left by 1 unit to the bottom-right corner dot.
- Interior: 2 dots are spaced along the middle horizontal level between the left indented vertex and the right boundary.

slope.instructions: TIMSS scaled this 2-point item with the generalized partial credit model (GPCM), which TIMSS uses for constructed-response items worth 2 or 3 points, in the calibration "Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 1995 and 2003 fourth-grade mathematics data". What is the item's slope (discrimination) parameter a? A higher a means that the item separates students of lower and higher mathematics ability more sharply. Choose the value closest to it. The state also lists reference items: the calibrated TIMSS items of the same grade most similar to this one (never the item itself or its other parts), most similar first, with their percent correct and their calibrated parameters, each on the scale of its own calibration. Use them to place this item.

location.instructions: TIMSS scaled this 2-point item with the generalized partial credit model (GPCM), which TIMSS uses for constructed-response items worth 2 or 3 points, in the calibration "Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 1995 and 2003 fourth-grade mathematics data". What is the item's location (difficulty) parameter b? b is on a logit scale on which the students of the calibration average about 0; a higher b means a harder item. Choose the value closest to it. The state also lists reference items: the calibrated TIMSS items of the same grade most similar to this one (never the item itself or its other parts), most similar first, with their percent correct and their calibrated parameters, each on the scale of its own calibration. Use them to place this item.

step1.instructions: TIMSS scaled this 2-point item with the generalized partial credit model (GPCM), which TIMSS uses for constructed-response items worth 2 or 3 points, in the calibration "Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 1995 and 2003 fourth-grade mathematics data". What is the item's step 1 parameter d1? In the GPCM, b - d1 is the ability at which earning the first point becomes more likely than earning no point, so a higher d1 means that this point is earned at a lower ability; the steps sum to 0. Choose the value closest to it. The state also lists reference items: the calibrated TIMSS items of the same grade most similar to this one (never the item itself or its other parts), most similar first, with their percent correct and their calibrated parameters, each on the scale of its own calibration.
